subject: physics

items.q: In a simple model of Earth's global mean energy flows, 340 W m⁻² of solar radiation arrives at the top of the atmosphere and 100 W m⁻² of this is scattered back to space by clouds, air and the surface. The surface emits 390 W m⁻² of infrared radiation. Earth is in energy equilibrium. What intensity of infrared radiation leaves Earth at the top of the atmosphere?
items.correct: 240 W m⁻²
items.misconception: 340 W m⁻²
items.why:
Simple diagrams of the greenhouse effect show one arrow of sunlight in and one arrow of infrared out, so the scattered fraction drops out of students' accounts; albedo is met as a separate idea and not written into the balance. Write the balance with every route: incoming solar power = scattered solar power + emitted infrared power. Only the absorbed part, (1 − α) × incoming, is re-emitted as infrared. For Earth, about 30% of the incoming 340 W m⁻² is scattered, so about 240 W m⁻² is emitted.

Working: At equilibrium the power leaving equals the power arriving (conservation of energy). Leaving = scattered solar radiation + emitted infrared, so emitted infrared = 340 W m⁻² − 100 W m⁻² = 240 W m⁻². The surface emission (390 W m⁻²) is not the outgoing value: most of it is absorbed by the atmosphere, which radiates both upwards and downwards.
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.random_wrong: 100 W m⁻²
items.working: At equilibrium the power leaving equals the power arriving (conservation of energy). Leaving = scattered solar radiation + emitted infrared, so emitted infrared = 340 W m⁻² − 100 W m⁻² = 240 W m⁻². The surface emission (390 W m⁻²) is not the outgoing value: most of it is absorbed by the atmosphere, which radiates both upwards and downwards.

items.q: In a simplified model of Earth's global mean energy flows, the surface absorbs 161 W m⁻² of solar radiation and 333 W m⁻² of infrared radiation emitted by the atmosphere. It loses 17 W m⁻² by convection and 80 W m⁻² by evaporation of water; the rest of its energy loss is by radiation. At the top of the atmosphere, 239 W m⁻² of infrared radiation leaves Earth. The surface is in equilibrium and can be treated as a black body. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, estimate the mean surface temperature.
items.why:
The 'blanket' picture of the greenhouse effect describes insulation that slows heat loss, so students write the surface's energy balance with sunlight as its only input. Every body above absolute zero radiates, and gases that absorb infrared also emit it. Include the atmosphere's downward emission as an input to the surface: in a global mean model, about 333 W m⁻² of back radiation arrives at the surface, compared with about 161 W m⁻² of absorbed sunlight.

Working: Surface energy balance. Absorbed = 161 + 333 = 494 W m⁻². Non-radiative losses = 17 + 80 = 97 W m⁻². Radiated intensity = 494 − 97 = 397 W m⁻² = σT⁴. T = (397 / 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = (7.00 × 10⁹ K⁴)^(1/4) = 289 K. (The 239 W m⁻² at the top of the atmosphere is not needed: it is the outgoing radiation from the surface–atmosphere system, not the surface's emission.)
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.working: Surface energy balance. Absorbed = 161 + 333 = 494 W m⁻². Non-radiative losses = 17 + 80 = 97 W m⁻². Radiated intensity = 494 − 97 = 397 W m⁻² = σT⁴. T = (397 / 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = (7.00 × 10⁹ K⁴)^(1/4) = 289 K. (The 239 W m⁻² at the top of the atmosphere is not needed: it is the outgoing radiation from the surface–atmosphere system, not the surface's emission.)

items.q: A simple model of Earth uses a solar constant of 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻² and an albedo of 0.30. The atmosphere absorbs none of the incoming solar radiation. The atmosphere, at a temperature of 242 K and with emissivity 0.780, radiates an intensity eσT⁴ upwards to space and an equal intensity downwards to the surface. The surface is a black body. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the equilibrium temperature of the surface?
items.why:
Greenhouse-effect diagrams draw the re-emitted radiation as an arrow pointing back at the ground, because that part explains the warming; the upward emission is often left out. A molecule has no preferred direction of emission. In a simple model the atmosphere emits εσT⁴ upwards and the same intensity downwards, and only the downward part is absorbed by the surface.

Working: Solar intensity absorbed by the surface = (1 − 0.30) × (1.36 × 10³ W m⁻²)/4 = 0.70 × 340 = 238 W m⁻². Intensity radiated downwards by the atmosphere = 0.780 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 242⁴ = 152 W m⁻². Surface equilibrium: σT⁴ = 238 + 152 = 390 W m⁻², so T = (390 / 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = 288 K. (Check: the atmosphere absorbs 0.780 × 390 = 304 W m⁻² of the surface's emission and emits 2 × 152 = 303 W m⁻², so it is also in balance, and 0.220 × 390 + 152 = 238 W m⁻² leaves to space.)
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.working: Solar intensity absorbed by the surface = (1 − 0.30) × (1.36 × 10³ W m⁻²)/4 = 0.70 × 340 = 238 W m⁻². Intensity radiated downwards by the atmosphere = 0.780 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 242⁴ = 152 W m⁻². Surface equilibrium: σT⁴ = 238 + 152 = 390 W m⁻², so T = (390 / 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = 288 K. (Check: the atmosphere absorbs 0.780 × 390 = 304 W m⁻² of the surface's emission and emits 2 × 152 = 303 W m⁻², so it is also in balance, and 0.220 × 390 + 152 = 238 W m⁻² leaves to space.)

items.q: In a climate model, a planet is initially in equilibrium. The concentration of carbon dioxide in its atmosphere is then suddenly increased and afterwards held constant. Immediately after the increase, the infrared intensity leaving the top of the atmosphere is 4 W m⁻² less than the solar intensity absorbed. The albedo does not change. What happens next in the model?
items.correct: The surface and atmosphere warm until the outgoing infrared again equals the solar intensity absorbed.
items.misconception: Nothing changes: energy is conserved, so the planet's energy and hence its temperature must stay the same.
items.why: 'Energy is conserved' is often remembered as 'energy stays the same', without the condition that the system is isolated. A planet exchanges energy with space by radiation, so it is not isolated. Apply conservation to the flows: rate of increase of stored energy = power absorbed − power emitted. An imbalance changes the internal energy of the oceans, land and air, and the temperature changes until the imbalance is removed.
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.random_wrong: The planet gains 4 W m⁻² for as long as the extra CO₂ is present, because the gas traps the energy.

items.q: Which statement about the emissivity of a surface is correct?
items.correct: It compares the power radiated per unit area with that of a black body at the same temperature.
items.misconception: It is the power radiated per unit area of the surface, so it is measured in watts per square metre.
items.why: The word sounds like 'emission', and emissivity is calculated from the radiated power per unit area, so students take it to be that power per unit area. e = (power radiated per unit area)/σT⁴. Two surfaces at different temperatures can have the same emissivity while radiating very different intensities.
items.specStatementText: emissivity as the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by a surface compared to that of an ideal black surface at the same temperature as given by emissivity = power radiated per unit area / σT⁴
items.random_wrong: It is the fraction of the incident radiation that the surface reflects, so it is equal to its albedo.

items.q: A planet orbits a star at a distance where the intensity of the star's radiation, the equivalent of the solar constant, is 2.40 × 10³ W m⁻². The planet's albedo is 0.40 and its emissivity is 0.80. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, estimate the planet's equilibrium temperature.
items.why:
Students use radiated power as a direct sign of temperature ('hotter things radiate more'), and when rearranging eσT⁴ = I they multiply by e instead of dividing. At equilibrium T = [I_absorbed/(eσ)]^(1/4). Emissivity is in the denominator: a smaller e gives a larger T. This is why an effective emissivity of about 0.6 for Earth corresponds to a surface warmer than 255 K.

Working: Mean absorbed intensity = (1 − 0.40) × (2.40 × 10³ W m⁻²)/4 = 0.60 × 600 = 360 W m⁻². Emitted intensity = eσT⁴. Equilibrium: 0.80 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × T⁴ = 360, so T⁴ = 360/(4.536 × 10⁻⁸) = 7.94 × 10⁹ K⁴ and T = 298 K.
items.specStatementText: emissivity as the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by a surface compared to that of an ideal black surface at the same temperature as given by emissivity = power radiated per unit area / σT⁴
items.working: Mean absorbed intensity = (1 − 0.40) × (2.40 × 10³ W m⁻²)/4 = 0.60 × 600 = 360 W m⁻². Emitted intensity = eσT⁴. Equilibrium: 0.80 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × T⁴ = 360, so T⁴ = 360/(4.536 × 10⁻⁸) = 7.94 × 10⁹ K⁴ and T = 298 K.

items.q: Which of the following defines the albedo of a planet?
items.correct: The total power scattered by the planet divided by the total power incident on it
items.misconception: The total power absorbed by the planet divided by the total power incident on it
items.why: Albedo appears in the same energy-balance equation as absorption and emission, and the word itself gives no clue to its meaning, so students attach it to the wrong term in (1 − α). A high albedo means strongly scattering: fresh snow (up to about 0.9) sends back most sunlight, while ocean (about 0.06) absorbs most of it. In the energy balance the absorbed intensity is (1 − α) × incident intensity.
items.specStatementText: albedo as a measure of the average energy reflected off a macroscopic system as given by albedo = total scattered power / total incident power
items.random_wrong: The power reflected by each square metre of the planet's surface, in W m⁻²

items.q: Sunlight of the same intensity falls on every part of a region of ocean. Cloud covers 30% of the region's area, and the cloud-covered part has an albedo of 0.60. The cloud-free 70% has an albedo of 0.06. What is the albedo of the region as a whole?
items.why:
Taking a plain mean is the default way students combine values, and the definition in terms of total scattered and total incident power is not used. Work from the definition: add the scattered powers of the parts, then divide by the total incident power. With the same intensity everywhere, the weights are the area fractions.

Working: Albedo = total scattered power / total incident power. For incident intensity I on a total area A: scattered power = 0.60 × (0.30IA) + 0.06 × (0.70IA) = (0.180 + 0.042)IA = 0.222IA. Albedo = 0.222IA / IA = 0.22.
items.specStatementText: albedo as a measure of the average energy reflected off a macroscopic system as given by albedo = total scattered power / total incident power
items.working: Albedo = total scattered power / total incident power. For incident intensity I on a total area A: scattered power = 0.60 × (0.30IA) + 0.06 × (0.70IA) = (0.180 + 0.042)IA = 0.222IA. Albedo = 0.222IA / IA = 0.22.

items.q: Satellite measurements show that the mean albedo of the polar regions is much higher than that of the tropical oceans. Which is the best explanation?
items.correct: Snow and ice cover much of the surface, and low-angle sunlight is reflected more strongly.
items.misconception: Snow and ice reflect all of the sunlight that falls on them, whereas ocean water reflects none of it.
items.why: Satellite images show cloud and ice as white and ocean as black, which suggests an all-or-nothing picture of reflection. Use each surface's own albedo: fresh snow scatters up to about 0.9 of incident sunlight, thick cloud roughly 0.5 to 0.8 and ocean about 0.06. The region's albedo is the power-weighted mean of these values.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.random_wrong: The polar regions are further from the Sun, so more of the sunlight that reaches them is reflected.

items.q: The albedo of a region of forest is measured from a satellite at the same time of day on two days, with the Sun at the same elevation. On day 1 the sky is clear and the albedo is 0.12. On day 2 thick cloud has formed over the region and the albedo is 0.48. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: The cloud scattered a larger fraction of the sunlight back to space, so less of it reached the forest.
items.misconception: The cloud absorbed and held the Sun's energy, and this trapped energy is what raised the albedo.
items.why: Students know that cloudy nights are warmer and that clouds 'keep heat in', and they apply this picture to daytime sunlight without distinguishing absorption from scattering. Albedo = scattered power / incident power, so only scattering raises it. Thick cloud scatters much of the incident sunlight back to space, so less reaches the surface below. The absorption and emission of infrared by clouds is a separate effect.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.random_wrong: A region's albedo is a fixed property of its surface, so one of the two readings must be a measurement error.

items.q: Which of the following is the solar constant?
items.correct: The intensity of sunlight above the atmosphere, on a surface perpendicular to the rays, at the mean Earth–Sun distance
items.misconception: The intensity of the Sun's radiation on a horizontal surface at ground level, averaged over a whole year at the equator
items.why: 'Sunlight at Earth' suggests sunlight where people are, on the ground, and school measurements of solar intensity are made at ground level. S is defined above the atmosphere, on a surface perpendicular to the rays, at the mean Earth–Sun distance, and is measured by satellites. The intensity at the ground is always less and varies with cloud and with the Sun's elevation.
items.specStatementText: the solar constant S
items.random_wrong: The total power emitted by the Sun in all directions, which stays constant from one year to the next

items.q: The solar constant at Earth, at a mean distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun, is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². Mars orbits the Sun at a mean distance of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m. What is the equivalent of the solar constant for Mars?
items.why:
Inverse proportion is the first relationship students meet for 'further away means less', and the squaring is easily forgotten. The Sun's power spreads over a sphere of area 4πd², which grows as d². Doubling the distance quarters the intensity.

Working: Intensity follows an inverse-square law, I = L/(4πd²), so S_Mars = S_Earth × (d_Earth/d_Mars)² = 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻² × (1.50/2.28)² = 1.36 × 10³ × 0.4328 = 589 W m⁻² = 5.89 × 10² W m⁻².
items.specStatementText: the solar constant S
items.working: Intensity follows an inverse-square law, I = L/(4πd²), so S_Mars = S_Earth × (d_Earth/d_Mars)² = 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻² × (1.50/2.28)² = 1.36 × 10³ × 0.4328 = 589 W m⁻² = 5.89 × 10² W m⁻².

items.q: The mean intensity of solar radiation incident on a planet's whole surface is S/4, where S is the solar constant. What is the origin of the factor of 4?
items.correct: The planet intercepts power over its cross-section πR², but this power is spread over its total surface area 4πR².
items.misconception: Half of the surface is in darkness at any instant, and half of the sunlight reaching the day side is reflected.
items.why:
Students look for two familiar reasons to halve and find night and reflection, instead of working through the geometry. Derive it: power intercepted = SπR²; surface area = 4πR²; mean intensity = S/4. Reflection is a separate factor: absorbed intensity = (1 − α)S/4, with α ≈ 0.30 for Earth, not 0.50.

Working: Power intercepted by the planet = S × (area of its projected disc) = SπR². This power is shared over the whole spherical surface, of area 4πR², so the mean incoming intensity = SπR²/4πR² = S/4.
items.specStatementText: that the incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4
items.random_wrong: The atmosphere absorbs or scatters three quarters of the Sun's radiation before it can reach the surface.
items.working: Power intercepted by the planet = S × (area of its projected disc) = SπR². This power is shared over the whole spherical surface, of area 4πR², so the mean incoming intensity = SπR²/4πR² = S/4.

items.q: Earth is modelled as a single black-body emitter with an albedo of 0.30, ignoring the greenhouse effect. The solar constant is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, estimate Earth's equilibrium temperature.
items.why:
S is described as 'the intensity of sunlight at Earth', and students picture every part of the surface facing the Sun, forgetting the night side and the oblique angle of the rays away from the point directly below the Sun. S applies to a surface perpendicular to the rays. Averaged over the whole spherical surface, the incoming intensity is S/4, about 340 W m⁻² for Earth, and the absorbed intensity is (1 − α)S/4.

Working: Energy balance: (1 − α)S/4 = σT⁴. Absorbed intensity = 0.70 × (1.36 × 10³ W m⁻²)/4 = 238 W m⁻². T = (238 / 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = (4.20 × 10⁹ K⁴)^(1/4) = 255 K.
items.specStatementText: that the incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4

items.q: Which statement about the main greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere is correct?
items.correct: Each of them has natural sources as well as sources in human activity.
items.misconception: Water vapour is not one of them, since it comes only from natural evaporation.
items.why: The greenhouse effect is usually met in discussions of human emissions, so 'greenhouse gas' becomes linked with 'man-made', and natural sources are assumed to have no effect. Every main greenhouse gas has natural and human sources, and molecules from both absorb identically. The natural greenhouse effect, due to naturally occurring gases, keeps Earth's mean surface about 33 K warmer than it would otherwise be; human activity adds to it.
items.specStatementText: that methane CH₄, water vapour H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, and nitrous oxide N₂O, are the main greenhouse gases and each of these has origins that are both natural and created by human activity
items.random_wrong: Nitrogen and oxygen are the main ones, as they make up about 99% of dry air.

items.q: Methane is released naturally from wetlands and also by human activity, for example livestock farming. Which statement about the absorption of infrared radiation by methane from these two sources is correct?
items.correct: Methane from both sources absorbs infrared identically, as absorption depends on the molecule.
items.misconception: Methane from farming absorbs more strongly, because it is released with pollutants that trap heat.
items.why: Media reports group 'emissions', 'pollution' and 'climate change' together, and exhaust fumes are the most visible human emissions. Classify gases by their physics: a greenhouse gas absorbs and emits infrared. Methane, water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide do this whatever their source, and pollution that causes smog or acid rain acts by different mechanisms.
items.specStatementText: that methane CH₄, water vapour H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, and nitrous oxide N₂O, are the main greenhouse gases and each of these has origins that are both natural and created by human activity
items.random_wrong: Only the methane from farming absorbs infrared; methane from wetlands is part of a natural balance.

items.q: A carbon dioxide molecule in the atmosphere absorbs an infrared photon emitted by Earth's surface. What happens?
items.correct: It moves to a higher vibrational energy level, and the energy is later emitted as infrared in all directions.
items.misconception: It reflects the photon, so that the infrared radiation is sent straight back down towards the Earth's surface.
items.why: The glass roof of a real greenhouse and textbook diagrams with arrows 'bouncing' off a layer of gas suggest reflection, which is the process students already use for light. Reflection returns radiation without absorbing it. Greenhouse gases absorb infrared (which is why only particular wavelengths are affected), are excited, and the energy is emitted in random directions, often after being shared in collisions.
items.specStatementText: the absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions
items.random_wrong: It moves to a higher energy level and then emits the infrared downwards, back to the surface.

items.q: In a simple model, a greenhouse-gas molecule in its ground state has one excited vibrational energy level, 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J above the ground state. Infrared photons of wavelengths 10.0 μm, 15.0 μm and 20.0 μm fall on such molecules. Which photons can be absorbed? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
items.correct: Only the photons of 15.0 μm
items.misconception: The photons of 10.0 μm and 15.0 μm
items.why:
In ionisation and the photoelectric effect there is a threshold and surplus energy becomes kinetic energy, so students carry the 'at least enough' rule over to transitions between bound energy levels. Transitions between bound levels need a match, hf = ΔE. This is why each greenhouse gas absorbs only at characteristic wavelengths, and why the clear atmosphere is largely transparent between about 8 μm and 13 μm.

Working: E = hc/λ. For 10.0 μm: (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(10.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁰ J. For 15.0 μm: 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J. For 20.0 μm: 9.95 × 10⁻²¹ J. Only the 15.0 μm photon energy equals the energy-level difference, so only those photons are absorbed.
items.specStatementText: the absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions
items.random_wrong: Photons of all three wavelengths
items.working: E = hc/λ. For 10.0 μm: (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(10.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁰ J. For 15.0 μm: 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J. For 20.0 μm: 9.95 × 10⁻²¹ J. Only the 15.0 μm photon energy equals the energy-level difference, so only those photons are absorbed.

items.q: According to the resonance model, how do greenhouse-gas molecules absorb infrared radiation?
items.correct: Radiation whose frequency equals a natural frequency of vibration of the bonds drives large vibrations.
items.misconception: Infrared photons carry more energy than visible ones, so they shake the molecules more violently.
items.why: Infrared is associated with the warmth felt from heaters and the Sun, so it seems powerful, while 'light' seems harmless. Use E = hc/λ: a 10 μm infrared photon has one twentieth of the energy of a 500 nm visible photon. Greenhouse gases absorb infrared because its photon energies match their vibrational energy-level spacings, not because the photons are energetic.
items.specStatementText: that the greenhouse effect can be explained in terms of both a resonance model and molecular energy levels
items.random_wrong: The molecules vibrate at whatever frequency the radiation has, so all are absorbed equally.

items.q: The bending vibration of a carbon dioxide molecule has a natural frequency of 2.0 × 10¹³ Hz, and carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation strongly at a wavelength of 15 μm. One student explains the absorption with a resonance model and another with molecular energy levels. Which statement correctly relates the two explanations? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
items.correct: Both are valid: the radiation's frequency is the natural frequency, and hf is the level spacing.
items.misconception: They contradict each other: one treats infrared as a wave, the other as photons, so only one is valid.
items.why:
Students expect a single 'true' model and see wave and photon descriptions of radiation as rivals, as in simplified accounts of the history of the wave–particle debate. Different models can describe the same phenomenon. Here both predict absorption at the same frequency: for the 15 μm band of CO₂, f = c/λ = 2.0 × 10¹³ Hz, and hf = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J is the vibrational energy-level spacing.

Working: f = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(15 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 2.0 × 10¹³ Hz, equal to the natural frequency (resonance model). Photon energy hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.0 × 10¹³ = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J, the spacing of the vibrational energy levels (energy-level model). Both models describe the same absorption.
items.specStatementText: that the greenhouse effect can be explained in terms of both a resonance model and molecular energy levels
items.random_wrong: Only the resonance model is valid, since energy levels belong to electrons in atoms, not to bonds.
items.working: f = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(15 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 2.0 × 10¹³ Hz, equal to the natural frequency (resonance model). Photon energy hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.0 × 10¹³ = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J, the spacing of the vibrational energy levels (energy-level model). Both models describe the same absorption.

items.q: What is meant by the enhanced greenhouse effect?
items.correct: The augmentation of the natural greenhouse effect by human activities that add greenhouse gases to the air
items.misconception: The greenhouse effect itself, which would not occur at all without the greenhouse gases released by human activity
items.why: The term is met almost only in discussions of human-caused climate change, so 'greenhouse effect' and 'enhanced greenhouse effect' are treated as the same thing. Distinguish the two. Without the natural greenhouse effect, and with the same albedo, Earth's mean surface temperature would be about 255 K rather than about 288 K. The enhanced effect is the additional warming from the extra greenhouse gases that human activity adds.
items.specStatementText: that the augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.random_wrong: Extra warming caused by holes in the ozone layer, which let more solar radiation through to the ground

items.q: At Mauna Loa, the annual mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rose from about 316 ppm (0.032%) in 1959 to about 421 ppm (0.042%) in 2023. Burning fossil fuels now releases more than 35 × 10⁹ tonnes of carbon dioxide per year; volcanoes release less than 1 × 10⁹ tonnes per year. Before industrialisation, the large natural exchanges of CO₂ between the air, the oceans and living things were approximately in balance. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: Burning fossil fuels is the main cause of the rise, and the extra CO₂ absorbs more of the surface's infrared.
items.misconception: Volcanoes are the main cause of the rise, because they release more CO₂ than human activity.
items.why: Eruptions are dramatic and widely reported, so their emissions are assumed to be large; the much larger but invisible emission from burning fuels is harder to picture. Compare the measured quantities: annual CO₂ emissions from burning fossil fuels are of the order of a hundred times those from volcanoes. Large natural flows of CO₂ between the air, the oceans and living things were approximately in balance before industrialisation, so fossil-fuel CO₂ is a net addition; the measured rise in atmospheric CO₂ is about half of fossil-fuel emissions, the rest being taken up by oceans and plants.
items.specStatementText: that the augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.random_wrong: The extra CO₂ has thinned the ozone layer, so more ultraviolet now reaches and heats the surface.

items.q: Do greenhouse gases stop energy leaving a planet, so that energy accumulates for as long as the gases are present?
items.correct: No. Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-emit it, and the planet still radiates to space. After an increase in greenhouse gases the planet warms only until the infrared power leaving again equals the absorbed solar power; its temperature is then steady.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases act like a lid that traps heat: infrared radiation cannot get out, so energy keeps building up while the gases are there.
items.why: The words 'greenhouse' and 'trap', and the image of a blanket or a glass roof, suggest a barrier that stops heat escaping rather than gases that absorb and emit radiation. A planet with greenhouse gases radiates to space all the power it absorbs from the Sun once it is in equilibrium; Earth emits about 240 W m⁻² of infrared to space. Greenhouse gases raise the surface temperature at which that balance is reached, because the surface also receives infrared from the atmosphere. They neither stop the outflow nor store energy indefinitely.
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the infrared radiation that leaves Earth to space the same radiation that the surface emits?
items.correct: No. Most of the surface's infrared emission is absorbed in the atmosphere, and much of the infrared leaving the top of the atmosphere is emitted by the atmosphere itself. The surface emits about 390 W m⁻², but only about 240 W m⁻² leaves to space.
items.misconception: The infrared radiation that leaves the top of the atmosphere is simply the radiation emitted by the surface, so the two intensities are equal.
items.why: Diagrams draw a single arrow from the ground straight out to space, and planets are first modelled as a single body with one temperature, so students do not separate the surface and the atmosphere as emitters. Treat the surface and the atmosphere as separate bodies. The surface's emission (σT⁴ at 288 K, about 390 W m⁻²) is larger than the outgoing infrared at the top of the atmosphere (about 240 W m⁻²) because the atmosphere absorbs most of it and radiates both upwards and downwards. Using the outgoing intensity to find the surface temperature gives about 255 K, not the observed 288 K.
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does Earth's surface lose energy to the atmosphere only by radiation?
items.correct: No. The surface also transfers energy to the atmosphere by convection (rising warm air) and by evaporation of water, whose latent heat is released when the vapour condenses in clouds.
items.misconception: In a climate energy balance, all the energy leaving the surface leaves as infrared radiation.
items.why: The greenhouse effect is taught as a story about radiation alone, and the Stefan–Boltzmann law is the only equation students apply to the surface, so convection and evaporation are left out. Subtract the non-radiative losses before applying the Stefan–Boltzmann law. The radiated intensity is the total absorbed intensity minus the energy carried away by convection and evaporation; only that remainder equals σT⁴ for a black-body surface.
items.specStatementText: the conservation of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are emissivity and albedo the same property of a surface?
items.correct: No. Albedo describes how much incident solar radiation is scattered back; emissivity compares the radiation a surface emits because of its own temperature with that from a black body. They enter the energy balance on opposite sides.
items.misconception: Emissivity and albedo both describe how a surface reflects radiation, so they are the same property and only one of them needs to be used.
items.why: Both are dimensionless numbers between 0 and 1 that describe how a surface interacts with radiation, and both are introduced in the same lesson. In (1 − α)(S/4) = eσT⁴, albedo reduces the absorbed intensity on the left and emissivity reduces the emitted intensity on the right. When both are given, use both.
items.specStatementText: emissivity as the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by a surface compared to that of an ideal black surface at the same temperature as given by emissivity = power radiated per unit area / σT⁴
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a white surface have a low emissivity because it is white?
items.correct: No. Emissivity for thermal (infrared) radiation does not follow visible colour. Snow and white paint have infrared emissivities close to 1, although they reflect most visible light.
items.misconception: Emissivity is set by a surface's visible colour: black surfaces have an emissivity near 1 and white surfaces an emissivity near 0.
items.why: The GCSE rule 'dull black surfaces are good emitters' is taught with examples in which visible colour and infrared behaviour happen to go together, so students generalise from what they can see. Colour describes behaviour at visible wavelengths. A surface at everyday temperatures emits in the infrared, and its emissivity there is a separate property. Snow is white, yet in the infrared it emits almost as a black body.
items.specStatementText: emissivity as the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by a surface compared to that of an ideal black surface at the same temperature as given by emissivity = power radiated per unit area / σT⁴
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does albedo have a unit such as W m⁻²?
items.correct: No. Albedo is a ratio of two powers, so it has no unit and lies between 0 and 1.
items.misconception: Albedo is the power reflected by each square metre of a surface, measured in W m⁻².
items.why: Energy-balance problems are full of intensities in W m⁻², and 'reflected power per square metre' sounds like the natural thing to measure, so students treat albedo as another intensity. Albedo = total scattered power / total incident power, a dimensionless ratio. The scattered intensity is albedo × incident intensity: for Earth, 0.30 × 340 W m⁻² ≈ 100 W m⁻².
items.specStatementText: albedo as a measure of the average energy reflected off a macroscopic system as given by albedo = total scattered power / total incident power
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the infrared radiation that Earth emits part of the sunlight it reflects?
items.correct: No. Scattered radiation is sunlight returned without being absorbed, mostly visible. Emitted radiation is infrared produced by Earth because of its own temperature. Albedo counts only the scattered part.
items.misconception: The radiation leaving Earth is reflected sunlight, so the infrared that Earth emits counts as part of its albedo.
items.why: Students' everyday model is that sunlight 'bounces off' the ground and leaves again, and both outgoing streams are drawn as similar arrows on diagrams. Separate the two outgoing streams: scattered short-wavelength sunlight, described by the albedo, and emitted long-wavelength infrared, described by the Stefan–Boltzmann law. The infrared is emitted only after absorbed energy has warmed the surface and atmosphere.
items.specStatementText: albedo as a measure of the average energy reflected off a macroscopic system as given by albedo = total scattered power / total incident power
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does albedo depend on how intense the incident sunlight is?
items.correct: No. Albedo is the ratio of scattered to incident power. Changing the incident power changes the scattered power in proportion; the ratio depends on the surface or cloud and on the angle of the rays.
items.misconception: Albedo is the amount of sunlight a place reflects, so it changes whenever more or less sunlight arrives.
items.why: Students think of albedo as an amount rather than a ratio, so they expect it to follow the brightness of the sunlight. Compare fractions, not amounts. Dimmer light on the same snow gives less scattered power but the same albedo. Earth's albedo varies because clouds, ice and the angle of the rays vary, not because the sunlight is brighter or dimmer.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do high latitudes differ from the tropics because they are further from the Sun?
items.correct: No. The difference in distance from the Sun between high and low latitudes (at most a few thousand kilometres out of 1.5 × 10⁸ km) is negligible. Latitude matters because of the angle at which the rays arrive and the snow and ice cover.
items.misconception: Places at high latitude are further from the Sun, so the sunlight arriving there is weaker and more of it is reflected.
items.why: Everyday experience that moving away from a fire feels cooler is extended to the Earth; the same reasoning lies behind the common belief that the seasons are caused by changing distance from the Sun. Earth's radius (6.4 × 10³ km) is about 1/23 000 of its distance from the Sun, so the inverse-square difference between latitudes is negligible. The effect of latitude comes from the low angle of the rays and from snow and ice.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do cold surfaces reflect more sunlight because they are cold?
items.correct: No. The fraction reflected depends on the material and texture of the surface and the angle of the rays, not on its temperature. Snow and ice reflect strongly because of their structure, not because they are cold.
items.misconception: The colder a surface is, the larger the fraction of radiation it reflects, so cold polar surfaces have a high albedo because of their low temperature.
items.why: The most reflective natural surfaces, snow and ice, are also the coldest, so a correlation is taken for a cause. Compare surfaces at the same temperature: fresh snow and dark rock at −10 °C have very different albedos. Albedo is a property of the material and its texture, together with the angle of the rays.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a region's or a planet's albedo a fixed value?
items.correct: No. Earth's albedo varies from day to day with cloud formation, and varies with latitude and season. The value 0.30 is a long-term global mean.
items.misconception: Albedo is a fixed property of a surface or planet, so a measured value different from the usual value must be an error.
items.why: Textbooks quote a single value, 0.30, in every calculation, so students treat it as a constant like σ. Treat 0.30 as an average. A region's albedo changes within hours as cloud forms or clears, and differs between the poles and the tropics.
items.specStatementText: that Earth’s albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the solar constant at a planet's distance found by dividing L/(4πd²) by 4?
items.correct: No. The solar constant is L/(4πd²): the intensity on a surface perpendicular to the rays, above the atmosphere, at the planet's mean distance from the Sun (about 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻² for Earth). Dividing by 4 gives S/4, the mean over the whole spherical surface, which is a different quantity.
items.misconception: The factor of 4 in S/4 belongs in the solar constant itself, so the intensity at a planet's distance is L/(4πd²) divided by 4.
items.why: S and S/4 appear together in energy-balance problems, and students remember that 'a quarter' is involved without knowing which of the two quantities it belongs to. Keep the two quantities apart. S = L/(4πd²) is the intensity at the planet's distance on a surface facing the Sun. The division by 4 that gives S/4 comes from spreading the power intercepted by the disc πR² over the sphere 4πR².
items.specStatementText: the solar constant S
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the solar constant the total power the Sun emits?
items.correct: No. The Sun's total power output is its luminosity, about 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. The solar constant is an intensity in W m⁻²: the luminosity divided by 4πd² at Earth's distance.
items.misconception: The solar constant is the total power emitted by the Sun, which does not change.
items.why: The name suggests a fixed property of the Sun itself, and the Sun's output is described as steady. Check the unit: S is in W m⁻², not W. S = L/(4πd²), so it depends on distance, and a planet further from the Sun has a smaller equivalent of the solar constant.
items.specStatementText: the solar constant S
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When the inverse-square law is used to find the intensity at a planet further from the Sun, which way up does the distance ratio go?
items.correct: The further planet receives less: I₂ = I₁(d₁/d₂)², with the smaller distance on top.
items.misconception: The square of the distance ratio multiplies the intensity whichever way up the ratio is written, so I₂ = I₁(d₂/d₁)² is equally valid.
items.why: Students remember that 'the square of the ratio' is involved but set up the ratio mechanically, without checking that a planet further out must receive less. Write I ∝ 1/d², so I₂/I₁ = (d₁/d₂)². Then check the answer: a planet further out than Earth must receive less than 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻².
items.specStatementText: the solar constant S
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Since half of a planet is lit at any time, is the mean incoming intensity S/2?
items.correct: No. Dividing by 2 allows for night but not for the rays striking the lit hemisphere obliquely. The lit hemisphere has an area of 2πR² but intercepts only SπR², so the mean over the whole surface is S/4.
items.misconception: Only the day side receives sunlight and it receives the full solar constant, so averaging over day and night gives S/2.
items.why: Day and night are the most obvious reason for averaging, and students picture the whole lit hemisphere as if it faced the Sun directly. The intercepted power is set by the disc πR² perpendicular to the rays. Spread over the day-side hemisphere 2πR² it gives a mean of S/2 there; spread over the whole sphere 4πR² it gives S/4.
items.specStatementText: that the incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mean incoming intensity S/4 because the atmosphere absorbs three quarters of the sunlight?
items.correct: No. S/4 is the mean intensity at the top of the atmosphere, averaged over the whole spherical surface. It arises from geometry, before any absorption in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: The atmosphere absorbs or scatters three quarters of the Sun's radiation, leaving S/4 to reach the surface.
items.why: S/4 is often quoted beside the observation that less sunlight reaches the ground than arrives at the top of the atmosphere, so students attach the factor to the atmosphere. Absorption and scattering are separate and much smaller than three quarters: about 30% of the incident sunlight is scattered back to space (the albedo), and roughly a fifth to a quarter is absorbed in the atmosphere. The factor 1/4 is πR²/4πR².
items.specStatementText: that the incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the 4 in S/4 come from the Sun's radiation spreading over a sphere of area 4πd²?
items.correct: No. The 4πd² gives the solar constant itself, the intensity at Earth's distance. The separate factor of 4 in S/4 comes from the planet: its surface area 4πR² divided by its cross-section πR².
items.misconception: The factor of 4 in S/4 is the 4 in 4πd²: the Sun's power spreads over a sphere and only a quarter of it reaches the planet.
items.why: Two different spheres, the Sun's sphere of radius d and the planet's sphere of radius R, each contribute a 4π, and students merge them. Keep the spheres apart. Sun: S = L/(4πd²). Planet: mean incoming intensity = SπR²/4πR² = S/4. The fraction of the Sun's power that reaches the planet is πR²/4πd², a tiny fraction, not a quarter.
items.specStatementText: that the incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are nitrogen and oxygen the main greenhouse gases, since they make up most of the atmosphere?
items.correct: No. Nitrogen and oxygen absorb almost no infrared radiation. The main greenhouse gases, CH₄, H₂O, CO₂ and N₂O, are present in much smaller amounts but absorb strongly at particular infrared wavelengths.
items.misconception: The gases present in the greatest amounts must have the greatest effect, so nitrogen and oxygen are the main greenhouse gases.
items.why: Students reason that a gas's effect is proportional to how much of it there is, and nitrogen and oxygen are the gases they know make up air. Whether a gas absorbs infrared depends on its molecular vibrations, not on its abundance. The two-atom molecules N₂ and O₂ do not absorb infrared significantly, so the greenhouse effect is due to much less abundant gases.
items.specStatementText: that methane CH₄, water vapour H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, and nitrous oxide N₂O, are the main greenhouse gases and each of these has origins that are both natural and created by human activity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide the only gas in the atmosphere that absorbs infrared radiation significantly?
items.correct: No. Methane, water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide are all main greenhouse gases, and water vapour makes the largest contribution to the natural greenhouse effect.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the greenhouse gas; the other gases in the atmosphere do not absorb infrared significantly.
items.why: Discussion of the enhanced greenhouse effect concentrates on CO₂ from fossil fuels, so students meet no other greenhouse gas by name. Learn the four main greenhouse gases named in the guide: CH₄, H₂O, CO₂ and N₂O. Each absorbs infrared at its own characteristic wavelengths, and an additional molecule of methane or nitrous oxide has a larger effect than an additional molecule of CO₂.
items.specStatementText: that methane CH₄, water vapour H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, and nitrous oxide N₂O, are the main greenhouse gases and each of these has origins that are both natural and created by human activity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does absorbing an infrared photon break a greenhouse-gas molecule apart?
items.correct: No. An infrared photon, with energy of order 10⁻²⁰ J, excites the molecule to a higher vibrational energy level. Breaking a bond in O₂ or CO₂ needs nearly 10⁻¹⁸ J (8.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J for O₂), which requires an ultraviolet photon.
items.misconception: When a greenhouse-gas molecule absorbs radiation, the energy breaks its bonds, and heat is released as the fragments move apart.
items.why: Students first meet absorption of radiation by gases in the chemistry of the ozone layer, where ultraviolet photons do split O₂ and O₃ molecules, and they apply the same picture to infrared. Resonance demonstrations, such as a glass shattered by sound, also suggest that driving a bond at its natural frequency breaks it. Compare the energies: a 15 μm photon has E = hc/λ = 1.3 × 10⁻²⁰ J, whereas breaking the O=O bond needs 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, over 60 times more. Absorbing an infrared photon changes the molecule's vibrational energy level and leaves the molecule intact.
items.specStatementText: the absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do greenhouse gases absorb all infrared radiation, whatever its wavelength?
items.correct: No. Each greenhouse gas absorbs only at particular wavelengths: those whose photon energies match its vibrational energy-level differences or, in the resonance model, whose frequencies match its natural frequencies.
items.misconception: Infrared radiation is heat, so greenhouse gases absorb it at every wavelength.
items.why: Infrared is introduced as 'heat radiation', so students treat it as one thing rather than a range of wavelengths and expect a 'heat-trapping' gas to absorb all of it. Infrared covers a wide range of wavelengths, from about 0.7 μm to 1 mm. CO₂ absorbs strongly near 15 μm, for example, while radiation near 10 μm passes through a clear, dry atmosphere largely unabsorbed.
items.specStatementText: the absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do greenhouse gases warm Earth by absorbing incoming sunlight?
items.correct: No. The main greenhouse gases are largely transparent to the visible light that carries most of the Sun's energy. They absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the surface.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases absorb the incoming sunlight, especially its ultraviolet, before it reaches the ground, and this is how they warm the planet.
items.why: The ozone layer, which does absorb incoming ultraviolet, is often confused with the greenhouse effect, and students assume the warming must come directly from the Sun's rays. Sunlight is mostly visible; Earth's emission is infrared. Greenhouse gases have energy-level spacings (natural frequencies) that match infrared photons, so they act on the outgoing radiation from the surface. If they blocked incoming sunlight, the surface would receive less energy, not more.
items.specStatementText: the absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the resonance model, does a molecule absorb every infrared frequency equally, since it vibrates at the frequency of the incoming radiation?
items.correct: No. A driven oscillator vibrates at the driving frequency, but its amplitude, and so the energy it absorbs, is large only when the driving frequency is close to its natural frequency.
items.misconception: Resonance just means the molecule vibrates at the frequency of the radiation, so every frequency is absorbed equally well.
items.why: Students learn that a driven system vibrates at the driving frequency and take this to be resonance, without the condition that the driving frequency must match the natural frequency. Resonance is the large response when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency. Far from it the amplitude is small and little energy is absorbed, which is why each gas absorbs only in particular bands.
items.specStatementText: that the greenhouse effect can be explained in terms of both a resonance model and molecular energy levels
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do discrete energy levels belong only to electrons in atoms?
items.correct: No. Molecules also have quantised vibrational energy levels. These are much more closely spaced than electron energy levels, which is why transitions between them involve infrared rather than visible or ultraviolet photons.
items.misconception: Discrete energy levels belong only to electrons in atoms, so the vibrations of a molecule can have any energy.
items.why: Energy levels are first taught through the hydrogen atom and atomic line spectra, so students tie quantisation to electrons alone. Any bound system has quantised energy. Molecular vibrational level spacings, of order 10⁻²⁰ J, correspond to infrared photons; electron energy-level spacings, of order 10⁻¹⁹ to 10⁻¹⁸ J, correspond to visible and ultraviolet photons.
items.specStatementText: that the greenhouse effect can be explained in terms of both a resonance model and molecular energy levels
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by the hole in the ozone layer?
items.correct: No. Ozone depletion lets more ultraviolet reach the surface, which harms living things, but it is a separate problem. The enhanced greenhouse effect is due to increased absorption of infrared by greenhouse gases.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases damage the ozone layer, and the hole lets in extra sunlight that heats the Earth.
items.why: Both are atmospheric problems linked to human emissions and are often taught together, and 'more radiation getting in' sounds like an explanation of warming. This is one of the most frequently reported confusions in research on students' ideas about the greenhouse effect. Keep the mechanisms separate. The ozone layer absorbs incoming ultraviolet, and its depletion, caused mainly by CFCs, matters for health. The enhanced greenhouse effect concerns the outgoing infrared from the surface, absorbed by CO₂, CH₄, N₂O and H₂O.
items.specStatementText: that the augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is global warming caused by the heat released when fuels are burned?
items.correct: No. The heat released directly by burning fuels is very small compared with the extra infrared absorbed because of the CO₂ produced. Burning fossil fuels enhances the greenhouse effect through the CO₂ it adds to the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Burning fuels warms the planet directly, through the heat released by engines, furnaces and power stations.
items.why: Burning visibly releases heat, so it is the most obvious link between using fuel and warming. Compare the effects per square metre of Earth's surface: the heat released by all human energy use averages a few hundredths of a W m⁻², whereas the additional greenhouse gases change the energy balance by a few W m⁻², roughly a hundred times more.
items.specStatementText: that the augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a gas that makes up less than 0.05% of the atmosphere have a significant effect on Earth's energy balance?
items.correct: Yes. What matters is how strongly the gas absorbs at the wavelengths at which Earth emits. CO₂ absorbs strongly near 15 μm, close to the peak of Earth's emission, so even at a few hundred parts per million it absorbs a large fraction of the surface's emission in that band.
items.misconception: A gas present in such a small proportion is too dilute to affect the absorption of infrared, so changes in its concentration cannot matter.
items.why: Students judge the effect of a substance by its proportion, as they do for the composition of air, rather than by how strongly each molecule absorbs. N₂ and O₂ make up about 99% of dry air and absorb almost no infrared; CO₂, at about 0.04%, absorbs strongly in its band. A small proportion of a strong absorber dominates absorption at its wavelengths, and raising its concentration increases the absorption.
items.specStatementText: that the augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect.
